question: Can sign-pattern structure in trained weights reveal the exact feature codes and Boolean computations of small neural networks without activation probes or learned dictionaries?

key_findings.claim: Feature channel coding represents each feature by a cross-neuron code and maps all inputs of a Boolean operation into the same output code, making individual neurons polysemantic while retaining a decodable circuit.
key_findings.evidence: The constructive account shows how ReLU neurons independently compute an AND on each code coordinate; partially overlapping codes permit superposition but inject channel interference.

key_findings.claim: Gradient-trained one-hidden-layer MLPs repeatedly learn the predicted sign-based channels on DNF variants, OR/CNF tasks, and a one-dimensional vision analogue.
key_findings.evidence: Static extraction from weight and bias sign categories recovers clauses and their input dependencies, including a counterintuitive DeMorgan-style solution for CNF and spatial feature codes in the toy vision task.

key_findings.claim: The Boolean experiments exhibit a capacity transition explained by the combinatorics of packing low-overlap feature codes rather than only parameter count.
key_findings.evidence: As formula complexity grows, the characteristic coding pattern becomes scarce, channel interference rises, and accuracy collapses; the paper derives limits for a specific four-positive-weight pattern and uses code counts as negative witnesses.

key_findings.claim: Weight trajectories gradually acquire the channel sign structure during optimization, linking the final combinatorial circuit to training dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: Checkpoint analysis tracks code statistics from random initialization through increasing structure and performance, showing the hypothesized channels emerge rather than merely being imposed by post-hoc thresholding.

key_findings.claim: Cascading feature disentanglement is a preliminary proposal for deeper models, not yet evidence that raw weight-sign analysis scales to modern networks.
key_findings.evidence: The paper factors conceptual layer transformations into decoding and coding matrices and demonstrates limited embedding/multi-output cases, while explicitly placing robust deep-network application in future work.

key_findings.claim: Exact recovery depends on a privileged Boolean basis and sign thresholding, so functionally equivalent reparameterizations can hide or alter the extracted code.
key_findings.evidence: All complete interpretations use small ReLU MLPs and hand-legible Boolean features; positive rescalings may preserve signs, but neuron rotations, normalization, residual mixing, and continuous features need not preserve the proposed combinatorial objects.

method.core_idea: Interpret neural computation through discrete positive/negative/zero patterns in weights and biases, treating low-overlap neuron subsets as feature-channel codes.
method.mechanism: Input features route into shared code coordinates; each coordinate redundantly performs the local Boolean operation; the output decodes the feature code; combinatorial extraction recovers dependency structure while code overlap predicts interference and capacity failure.
assumptions: Relevant computations admit discrete Boolean features and shallow ReLU implementations.
Weight signs and near-zero thresholds are stable and semantically meaningful.
Features use redundant cross-neuron codes with limited overlap.
The trained network selects the hypothesized coding family rather than an equivalent alternative.
Layerwise disentanglement can recover useful bases in deeper networks.

techniques.role: Discretizes learned parameters into combinatorial positive, negative, and zero structures.
Represents a feature by a shared subset/sign pattern across neurons.
Relates low-overlap code capacity to formula complexity and error.
Recovers feature dependencies directly from trained weights without activation data.
Proposes a layerwise route to undo mixed coding and decoding in deeper networks.

evaluations.setting: Small single-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs trained on positive/negated DNF, OR, and CNF Boolean functions.
evaluations.metric: Recovered feature channels, sign-pattern frequency, exact dependency interpretation, and task error.
evaluations.result: Predicted coding patterns appear far above random expectation and support complete circuit descriptions in the showcased models.
evaluations.baseline: Random sign structures and activation-space-only interpretation.

evaluations.setting: Increasing Boolean formula size relative to hidden width.
evaluations.metric: Code-packing feasibility, interference, and accuracy transition.
evaluations.result: Loss of usable low-overlap codes coincides with representational collapse, yielding a mechanism-level account of the observed scaling boundary.
evaluations.baseline: Parameter-count scaling without a coding mechanism.

evaluations.setting: One-dimensional synthetic vision task and limited embedding/multi-output networks.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy of extracted feature codes and qualitative circuit recovery.
evaluations.result: The same coding lens recovers spatial feature structure, while deeper-network evidence remains preliminary.

limitations: Complete results are confined to small synthetic networks and mostly one hidden layer.
Boolean features and a known task grammar make ground-truth interpretation unusually favorable.
Thresholding continuous weights into sign categories introduces an analysis hyperparameter.
The representation is not shown invariant to common function-preserving reparameterizations.
Cascading disentanglement is not validated on transformers, convolutional networks, or natural data.
Capacity theory is derived for specific coding patterns rather than all algorithms available to a network.
failure_modes: Dense overlapping codes can make static extraction ambiguous and computation inaccurate.
A trained network may switch to a non-channel algorithm instead of following the predicted collapse.
Neuron rotations or cross-layer residual mixing can destroy legible sign patterns without changing behavior.
Continuous and multidimensional features may not admit discrete code membership.
Near-zero weights can change category under noise, quantization, or retraining.
reusable_insights: Interpretability can exploit discrete parameter structure in addition to activation geometry.
A mechanistic scaling law should name the representational resource that saturates.
Static weight hypotheses should be checked against training trajectories and randomized nulls.
Polysemantic neurons can coexist with monosemantic distributed channels.
open_questions: Do feature-channel codes appear in convolutional or transformer circuits trained on natural data?
Can code extraction be made invariant to neuron permutation, rescaling, and broader reparameterizations?
How should continuous or compositional features be encoded combinatorially?
Can cascading disentanglement be automated and independently validated?
Do code-packing statistics predict scaling transitions before task error changes?

competitive_landscape.title: Toy Models of Superposition
competitive_landscape.difference: Elhage et al. explain polysemanticity through overcomplete activation directions and polytope geometry; the target replaces feature directions with discrete cross-neuron codes and adds an explicit Boolean computation mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Cunningham et al. learn sparse activation directions at language-model scale; the target avoids auxiliary dictionaries and recovers exact shallow Boolean dependencies from parameters, but has not reached comparable model/data scale.

competitive_landscape.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
competitive_landscape.difference: Transcoders learn sparse replacements for MLPs and extract circuits in models up to 1.4B parameters; the target offers a training-free static decoder for toy networks and a different combinatorial ontology.

competitive_landscape.title: Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
competitive_landscape.difference: APD learns additive parameter components optimized for faithfulness, minimality, and simplicity; the target reads pre-existing sign patterns without training a decomposition and focuses on exact Boolean channel codes.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Combinatorial weight analysis yields exact mechanistic interpretations and the first mechanism-level explanation of a parameter-capacity scaling boundary in the studied tasks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Static sign-based extraction, randomized pattern comparisons, training trajectories, code-packing analysis, and multiple Boolean variants agree in shallow networks.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The feature-channel computation account is genuinely distinct from activation-direction superposition and APD. Its importance depends on whether the discrete codes survive natural tasks, depth, and reparameterization; those are not yet demonstrated.
